journal_name: IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing

abstracts.abstract: Self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for speech representation learning, yet existing approaches fundamentally rely on contrastive or predictive objectives that may not adequately capture the hierarchical linguistic structure inherent in speech signals. This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, termed Hierarchical Information-theoretic Speech Encoding (HISE), which reconceptualizes speech representation learning through the lens of information bottleneck theory and variational Bayesian inference. We formalize the problem by establishing rigorous mathematical connections between information-theoretic measures and linguistic invariance, subsequently deriving an optimization objective that simultaneously captures phonemic, prosodic, and semantic information at multiple temporal scales. The theoretical contributions include three key results: first, we prove the representational sufficiency of hierarchical consistency constraints for guaranteeing linguistic invariance; second, we develop a tractable variational approximation enabling end-to-end optimization; third, we provide an information-theoretic analysis characterizing the trade-off between compression and preservation of task-relevant information. Experiments on zero-shot phoneme recognition and spoken language understanding demonstrate that HISE representations exhibit superior cross-lingual transfer capabilities, outperforming established baselines including wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT by margins of 3.2% and 2.8% respectively. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for self-supervised speech processing that fundamentally differs from existing paradigms by emphasizing hierarchical information structure rather than single-level prediction.

Transformer-based architectures have become dominant in automatic speech recognition, yet the quadratic computational complexity of self-attention mechanisms presents significant challenges for processing long-form audio content. This paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of attention sparsity patterns in speech recognition systems, deriving optimal sparsity constraints that preserve critical acoustic-phonetic information while eliminating redundant computations. We first establish a formal framework characterizing the relationship between attention weight distributions and linguistic boundaries, demonstrating both analytically and empirically that attention patterns exhibit structured sparsity correlated with phoneme transitions. Building upon this analysis, we prove that constraining attention to linguistically meaningful spans maintains model capacity while reducing computational overhead. The theoretical analysis yields three primary insights: the optimal sparsity ratio depends on the acoustic characteristics of the input, attention sparsity and language model perplexity exhibit a predictable inverse relationship, and positional encoding schemes significantly impact the structure of attention patterns. Based on these findings, we propose Adaptive Sparse Attention (ASA), which dynamically adjusts attention patterns according to acoustic-phonetic boundaries. Experiments on LibriSpeech and Switchboard corpora demonstrate that ASA achieves relative WER improvements of 8.3% and 6.7% respectively while reducing computational complexity by approximately 70%. This work provides a principled theoretical basis for efficient transformer design in speech recognition.

Conventional spoken dialogue systems process speech and language sequentially, first performing automatic speech recognition to generate text transcriptions and subsequently applying natural language understanding to extract meaning. This cascaded pipeline architecture introduces several fundamental limitations: error propagation between stages, loss of prosodic and paralinguistic information during transcription, and increased latency from multi-stage processing. This paper introduces INTEGRA, an innovative integrated speech-language architecture that fundamentally reconceptualizes spoken dialogue processing as a unified multimodal transduction problem. Rather than maintaining separate specialized modules, INTEGRA processes acoustic waveforms directly to generate dialogue responses through a single differentiable architecture. The system comprises three key components: a hierarchical multimodal encoder that jointly represents acoustic and textual features at phonemic, lexical, and semantic levels; a cross-modal fusion mechanism that preserves paralinguistic information throughout processing; and a response generator that produces both verbal content and appropriate prosodic contours. The design philosophy emphasizes that speech carries information beyond textual content that dialogue systems should leverage. Evaluation on the DSTC11 benchmark suite demonstrates that INTEGRA achieves state-of-the-art performance across task-oriented and conversational domains, with particular improvements in error robustness under noisy conditions and response appropriateness. This paradigm shift from cascaded to integrated speech-language processing establishes a new direction for spoken dialogue system research.

Emotion recognition from speech presents significant challenges due to the subtle and context-dependent nature of affective vocal expressions. Existing approaches typically employ pre-defined discrete emotion categories that fail to capture the continuous, multidimensional nature of emotional experience. This paper presents EmoSpan, a novel system for continuous emotion prediction that models emotional states as dynamic trajectories in a learned multidimensional affective space rather than static categorical assignments. The proposed architecture employs a multi-task learning framework that jointly optimizes for categorical emotion classification, dimensional attribute regression, and emotion segment boundary detection using a unified set of parameters. The system processes acoustic features through a temporal convolutional network augmented with self-attention to capture long-range dependencies in emotional expression, while a novel span extraction module identifies emotionally coherent segments for more interpretable predictions. A critical innovation is the incorporation of speaker normalization that adapts emotion representations to individual speaking styles, significantly improving recognition accuracy for atypical speakers. Extensive experiments on the IEMOCAP, MELD, and CREMA-D datasets demonstrate that EmoSpan achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving categorical accuracy by 5.4% absolute on IEMOCAP and reducing continuity prediction error by 18% compared to previous best systems. The system operates in real-time with latency suitable for interactive applications.
